image_description: A low-angle, close-up view of the underside and support structure of a large white radio telescope dish. The image highlights the complex steel lattice truss system supporting the parabolic reflector. A white rectangular equipment box (likely housing receivers or electronics) is mounted on the central structure. The background shows a pale sky and hints of other structural elements.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Enormous parabolic dish antenna of colossal scale, dwarfing all surrounding structures.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The perspective looking up at the massive lattice structure implies a colossal scale typical of radio telescopes. The curvature of the rim visible at the top confirms the parabolic dish shape.
The upper edge of the frame shows a distinct, smooth arc consistent with a parabolic reflector's geometry.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Massive installation spanning an area visible from great distances.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The image is a tight close-up of the internal structure; the full span and external context are not visible to verify 'great distance' visibility.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Receiver feed horn at focal point of dish.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The image shows the back/support side of the dish. The feed horn is typically located in front of the dish (at the focal point) or on a boom extending over the face, which is not visible in this rear-structure shot.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Alt-azimuth or equatorial mount for celestial tracking.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The heavy-duty central pivot and truss connections visible in the center are characteristic of the mounting mechanism required for such a large instrument.
The mechanical joints and symmetrical truss design imply rotational capability around the vertical axis.
The image is angled upwards; the ground-level foundation is completely out of frame.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Metal mesh or solid aluminum panel dish surface.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Through the gaps in the white support trusses, the greyish backing of the dish surface is visible, appearing to be metal panels or mesh.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Astronomical instrument for detecting radio-frequency emissions.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The overall structure matches the known visual signature of a radio telescope.
Same as the alt-azimuth mount checkpoint; the robust central engineering supports this function.

artifact_observations.location: Central truss intersections and lower-left lattice work
artifact_observations.reasoning: Several struts appear to merge or fade into each other without clear bolted or welded joints. In the lower left, some diagonal braces seem to terminate abruptly or blend into the background sky, lacking physical continuity.

The texture is overly smooth and uniform, lacking the subtle variations in paint thickness, rust spots, or weathering expected on a large outdoor industrial structure. It has a slight 'plastic' or rendered look.

The curvature of the dish rim seems slightly inconsistent with the perspective of the internal trusses, appearing somewhat flattened or warped rather than following a perfect geometric arc relative to the camera angle.

selected_experts.reason: To confirm the specific class identity and rule out generic 'antenna' or 'satellite dish' misclassifications.
To verify the 3D spatial relationships of the overlapping lattice beams and ensure no impossible depth ordering or melting occurs.
To check for disconnected segments or fused beams in the complex truss network where visual clutter is high.
To assess the realism of lighting, shadows, and material textures on the white steel surfaces.

focus_areas: Connectivity of truss joints (look for floating or merging beams)
Consistency of parabolic curvature across the visible rim
Realism of paint texture and weathering on steel
Logical occlusion of background elements through the lattice
